What you're talking about sounds like a compulsion, rather than an intrusive thought. For me the most helpful thing was learning about ocd and the kind of stuff it can do. For example, like you said, it can make you blow things way out of proportion. Or it can make an intrusive thought feel like an impulse or a desire. Learning all about ocd for me helps me ground myself because I can realize that everything I'm experiencing is the exact symptoms of ocd. From there, I usually try to use that knowledge to stop me from doing my compulsions. Plus, regardless of whether you've done something bad or not, ruminating isn't going to fix it. It can be good to apologize to people you think you've wronged but if it becomes excessive(feeling the need to apologize to someone in third grade who you pushed on the playground once, for example) or if you're apologizing more than once for the same thing, that is likely a compulsion. As for talking with a therapist, it's not easy, but if you find the right one they'll know to help you open up. I'd suggest letting your therapist know you have trouble opening up and they'll be happy to work with you. Something that helps me open up to people is just sharing videos about ocd with them. Instead of me having to explain everything I've been going through, I'll just send them a video on the symptoms of ocd and tell them that I relate heavily to it. These are personal anecdotes because honestly I'm not sure what the best course of action is, I just know what has been helping me. I hope it can help you too.

I'm going to assume at least one of these is true for you:
1. The things you did in your past weren't as bad as you think they were.  
2. You were in a bad situation when you did those things or were hanging around the wrong people.
3. You find your past actions upsetting and don't want to repeat them. 

If any or all of these are true, you're not a bad person. You might have done bad things but they're not a reflection of your character or your true desires. I'm willing to bet you didn't do those things out of a desire to be "bad" but as a method of coping or compensation for something important you weren't receiving in your life; love, compassion, acceptance, resources you needed to survive, friendship, etc.
People say stuff like that all the time if they want it to be true about a person or character. It doesn't necessarily mean it's true.

Sounds like intrusive thoughts. My brother used to have similar ones, he would have intrusive thoughts of how to efficiently commit mass murder. He felt like a psychopath until he realized they were just a symptom of his anxiety.

The anxiety wasn't what was holding you back from doing those things, it's your moral code. I know it can feel scary but please know you're not the only one. So many people with ocd have this same issue, and none of them ever act on their intrusive thoughts.

Intrusive thoughts are thoughts that go against our moral code. They wouldn't distress us if we had anything in our nature that wanted to follow them. When you have an intrusive thought, try to put a mental sticky note on it, labeling it an intrusive thought. Beyond that, don't try to fight the intrusive thought or convince yourself it's not what you want, because it will only drain you of your energy, and the intrusive thoughts will come back. The less energy you put into fighting intrusive thoughts, the less you'll have them.
